body.p: Applicant has amended and clarified the application to place the application, as a whole, into prima facie condition for allowance at this time. In particular, Applicant has added claim 77. Applicant submits that substantial care has been taken to avoid the introduction of any new subject matter into the application as a result of the foregoing amendments.1

Claims 1, 59-65, 68, 73, 75-76 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102 as being anticipated by United States Patent Application Publication No. 2010/0253129 published in the name of Dowty, and claims 1 and 66 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102 as being anticipated by United States Patent No. 6,412,870 issued to Higgins. Applicant has carefully considered the rejections under 35 U.S.C. §102 set forth on pages 2-7 of the Office Action, and Applicant respectfully submits that the cited prior art cannot anticipate the aircraft seats of independent claim 1, and all associated dependent claims, as previously presented, for at least the following reasons.

Dowty discloses a passenger seat 100 comprising a deployment mechanism 10 that coordinates movement of a seat pan 20, a leg rest 30 and a seat back 40. The deployment mechanism 10 is driven by a single linear actuator 12 that forcibly extends to drive the passenger seat toward a maximally reclined configuration (illustrated in Figures 2 and 3 copied below). The passenger seat 100 is supported by a rigid frame 110 having upright leg assemblies 112 and tubular horizontal beams 114.

Thus the yoke 32 is constrained to pivot about the pin 122 relative to the frame.

The actuator 12 is pivotally connected at opposing ends thereof to the rigid frame 110 and the drive link 14. The drive link 14 forces the yoke 32 to pivot about the pin 122, thereby extending the distal end 34 of the yoke from the stowed TTL position of FIG. 1 to the deployed configuration of FIG. 3, as the
actuator 12 extends to adjust the seat 100 toward the reclined configuration.

[0020] As shown when FIGS. 1-3 are taken sequentially, as the actuator 12 extends, pivoting the yoke 32 and raising the distal end 34 of the yoke, the leg rest 30 is deployed by the leg support link 36 toward a leg supporting position
by pivoting about the forward end of the seat pan 20.

[0022] Simultaneously with the deployment of the leg rest 30 as the actuator 12 extends, the seat pan 20 is pulled forward by the upper end 38 of the leg rest 30. Movement of the seat pan 20 is guided by a seat pan link 26 and a roller that bears upon the lower surface of the seat pan. When the actuator 12 extends to recline the seat 100, the seat pan link 26 guides the seat pan 20 forward, by approximately 4 inches in one particular example, with respect to the stationary frame 110. In moving from its TTL position in FIG. 1 to its maximally reclined position in FIG. 3, the seat pan moves forward overall, with its forward end raising and its rearward end lowering for the comfort of a seated
passenger.
In the Office Action, the Examiner considers that the seat pan link 26 of the seat 100 disclosed
in Dowty forms a first pivoting connection to mount the seat pan to the seat chassis. The
Examiner goes on to consider that the bottom pivot pin point of the seat pan link 26 constitutes
a seat pan pivot axis within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application. The seat pan link

26 has a top pivot pin point connected to the seat pan 20; and a bottom pivot pin point connected to the rigid frame 120. The pivoting motion of the seat pan link 26 is illustrated in Figures 2 and 3. However, contrary to the Examiner's comments, the seat pan 20 does not pivot about the bottom pivot pin point of the seat pan link 26. As outlined in paragraph [0022], the seat pan 20 is pulled forward by the upper end 38 of the leg rest 30. The forward motion of the seat pan 20 is guided by the seat pan link 26, but there is no hint or suggestion that the seat pan 20 pivots about the bottom pivot pin point. As such, Applicant respectfully submits that the bottom pivot pin point does not constitute "a seat pan pivot axis about which the seat pan pivots."

Furthermore, the top pivot pin point of the seat pan link 26 cannot be considered as constituting a seat pan pivot axis within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application. The location of the top pivot pin point changes as the seat pan 20 travels forwards. In contrast, claim 1 of the present application expressly requires that the location of the seat pan pivot axis is fixed relative to the seat chassis. Thus, the top pivot pin point does not form a seat pan pivot axis within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application. It is noted also that the seat pan link 26 is not connected to the seat pan 20 in front of the connection formed by the top pivot pin point.

The Examiner further states that the y-shaped leg rest pivot yoke 32 is a seat pan link within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application. Claim 1 includes further requires that the at least one seat pan link "is coupled to the seat pan in front of the seat pan pivot axis." The Examiner considers that the pin 122 (shown in Figures 2 and 3) couples the y-shaped leg rest pivot yoke 32 to the seat pan 20. Applicant respectfully submits that Dowty does not, in any way, disclose this arrangement. As outlined in paragraph [0019], the y-shaped leg rest pivot yoke 32 "is pivotally attached to the forward end of the frame 110 by a pin 122." The connection of the y-shaped leg rest pivot yoke 32 to the frame 110 is most clearly shown in Figure 2 in which the seat pan 20 is spaced apart from the pin 122.

The Examiner has also cited Higgins as anticipating at least claim 1 of the present application. Higgins discloses a seating unit 10 comprising fixed armrest units 76, 78, a seating portion 80, a seat back 82 and a leg rest 84. The operation of the seating unit 10 is illustrated in Figures 9, 10 and 11 (copied below). A rear transverse member 98 and a front transverse member 108, together with other structural elements (not shown, which may include the floor of the aircraft) form a base for the seat.
Higgins further discloses:

A front support strut 100 has its upper end connected by a pivot pin 101 to a location on the seat portion 80 spaced forwardly from the hinge 86. The lower end of the strut 100 is connected by a pivot pin 102 to one end of an L-shaped lifter link 104 which is supported at its mid-point on a pivot pin 106. The pin 106 is mounted on a front transverse member 108 extending between the side panels 76. The other end of the lifter link 104 is connected to a first screw jack drive 110 mounted between the side panels 76. A second screw jack drive 112 is mounted between the side panels 76 and has its driven end connected by a pivot pin 114 to an intermediate location on the front support strut 100. (See
column 3, lines 37 to 48.)

The leg rest 84 is connected to the seat portion 82 by a four-bar link mechanism comprising links 116 and 118 which are pivotally connected to the seat portion 80 and links 120 and 122 which are pivotally connected to the leg rest 84. The link 118 is connected by a first intermediate pivot pin 124 to the link 120 and by a second intermediate pivot pin 126 to the link 122. The link 120 is also connected by a third intermediate pivot pin 128 to the link 116. The link 120 has an infill panel 130 rigidly mounted thereon for a purpose to be explained hereinafter. A third screw jack drive 132 is mounted on the front support strut 110 and has its driven end connected by a pivot pin 134 to an intermediate point
on the link 118. (See column 3, lines 53 to 65.)

When it is desired to move the seat from the upright position shown in FIG. 9 to an intermediate reclined position as shown in FIG. 10, the second screw jack drive 112 drives the front support strut 100 forwards so that the slider 88 starts to move along the guide track 90. If it is desired to deploy the leg rest 84 at the same time, the third screw jack drive 132 pushes the link 118 forwards. (See
column 3, line 66 to column 4, line 5.)
The Examiner considers that the connection between the seat portion 80 and the strut 100
(defined by the pivot pin 101) forms a seat pan pivot axis within the meaning of claim 1 of the
present application. As outlined above, claim 1 recites: "the location of the seat pan pivot axis
being fixed relative to the seat chassis." In respect of this feature, the Examiner references the
disclosure of Higgins that the pivot pin is mounted between the side panels of the chassis. The
Examiner cites column 6, lines 38-45 in relation to this statement, but this encompasses claims
19 and 20 which are unrelated to this feature. As such, it is not evident which section of Higgins
is considered by the Examiner to be material to this feature. It is noted that Higgins describes
the pin 106 as being "mounted on a front transverse member 108 extending between the side

panels 76." (See column 3, lines 42 and 43.) However, the pin 106 defines the pivot axis of the L-shaped lifter link 104. For the avoidance of all doubt, there is nothing to suggest that the seat portion 80 pivots about the pin 106.

Applicant respectfully submits that Higgins does not disclose a seat pan pivot axis which is fixed relative to the seat chassis. Contrary to the requirement of claim 1, the pivot pin 101 travels relative to the seating unit 70 as the configuration of the seating unit 10 changes. This movement is apparent in Figures 9, 10 and 11 which show the pivot pin 101 travelling along a circular arc centered on the pivot pin 102 disposed at the opposite end of the strut 100. Moreover, the pivot pin 102 travels as the first screw jack drive 110 is actuated to pivot the L- shaped lifter link 104 about the pivot pin 106. Neither the pivot pin 101 nor the pivot pin 102 can be considered as a seat pan pivot within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application.

Higgins discloses that the leg rest 84 is connected to the seat portion 82 by a four-bar link mechanism comprising links 116 and 118 which are pivotally connected to the seat portion 80 and links 120 and 122 which are pivotally connected to the leg rest 84. The Examiner considers that the link 118 constitutes a seat pan link within the meaning of claim 1 of the present application. The link 118 is pivotally connected to the seat portion 80. The link 118, in combination with the third screw jack drive 132, control the deployment of the leg rest 84. Higgins teaches: "If it is desired to deploy the leg rest 84 at the same time, the third screw jack drive 132 pushes the link 118 forwards." (See column 4, lines 4 and 5.) The operation of the link 118 and the third screw jack drive 143 is independent of the other control functions of the seating unit 10. Applicant respectfully submits that the link 118 is unrelated to the pivoting motion of the seat pan 80. As such, the link 118 cannot reasonably be construed as "at least one seat pan link for controlling pivoting of the seat pan about said seat pan pivot axis" (emphasis added).

The Examiner further posits that the link 120 disclosed in Higgins constitutes a leg rest link according to the present invention. The Examiner notes that the link 120 is connected to the leg rest 84 and the link 116 (which also forms part of the four-bar link mechanism for connecting the leg rest 84 to the seat portion 82). The Examiner would appear to be citing two different links (links 116 and 118) as forming the seat pan link. Applicant respectfully submits that this approach is inappropriate. Moreover, we reiterate the above comment that neither link 116, nor link 118 is suitable for controlling pivoting of the seat pan about said seat pan pivot axis. Applicant respectfully submits that these links do not constitute a seat pan link within the meaning of the present invention.
Contrary to the requirement of claim 1 of the present application, Higgins does not disclose at least one seat pan link "coupled to the seat pan in front of the seat pan pivot axis."

In light of the foregoing clarifications, Applicant respectfully submits that independent claim 1, and all associated dependent claims, now even more fully satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. §102. Applicant respectfully requests favorable reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection of the above-identified claims under 35 U.S.C. §102 based upon the cited prior art of record.

Claims 67, 69-72, and 74 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over the cited prior art of record. Applicant has carefully considered the rejection of claims 67, 69-72, and 74 under 35 U.S.C. §103 set forth on pages 7-12 of the Office Action, and without, in any way, conceding to the propriety of these rejections, Applicant respectfully submits that the above-identified cited prior art cannot render obvious the aircraft seats of the above-identified claims, as clarified, for at least the following reasons. With regard to claims 67, 69-72, and 74, and for the purpose of avoiding prolix, Applicant hereby incorporates its arguments submitted supra pertaining to the deficiencies of the teachings of the cited prior art.
In light of the foregoing clarifications, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 67, 69-

72, and 74, now even more fully satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. §103. Applicant respectfully requests favorable reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection of the above- identified claims under 35 U.S.C. §103 based upon the cited prior art of record.
Applicant has added claim 77 and respectfully submits it introduces no new matter, is patentable over the prior art of record, and is otherwise proper.

The Office Action Summary indicates that the drawings file on July 19, 2023, are objected to by the Examiner. No information is provided as to the nature of this objection. Moreover, Applicant submits that the corresponding section in the Office Action dated December 7, 2023, indicated that the same drawings were accepted by the Examiner. As such, clarification is respectfully solicited.
